The high-level idea of searching over semantic strategies rather than raw code is intuitive and potentially impactful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/a3652d5e47ca42e58fea85ccca7438b3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

SEVEX combines an abstract idea tree, novelty-aware selection, empirical execution, and semantic feedback in a coherent closed-loop system. The distinction between conceptual strategies and their code implementations is sensible for controlling context length and search complexity.

The reported primary-model results are promising: average accuracy rises from 71.6% for naive inference and 64.6% for SketchPad to 78.9%, while inference-time token usage remains close to naive inference and far below per-sample code generation.

The experiments span nine tasks from two perception-oriented benchmarks, and the paper reports both effectiveness and token costs. Five-run learning curves for two tasks provide some evidence that the search components improve exploration stability.

The qualitative examples are informative. In particular, using typographic reference lines for CircledLetter and depth-map discontinuities for Jigsaw illustrates that the framework can discover nontrivial ways of repurposing visual tools.
The paper is generally well organized, and the diagrams, tables, development-set indices, tool inventory, and several agent prompts aid understanding.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is too narrow for the central algorithmic claim. The main study uses only naive inference, SketchPad, and a text-prompt-optimized SketchPad variant. It does not compare against fixed visual-scaffolding methods discussed in related work, random or greedy semantic search, standard UCT, best-of-N agent generation, or other program-search/agent-optimization approaches under matched budgets. Thus it is unclear whether the gain comes from the proposed NUCT and semantic backpropagation rather than simply performing 50 rounds of task-specific search.

The main nine-task evaluation uses only Gemini-2.5-Flash, apparently with a single exploration run per task. The five-run ablation is restricted to Jigsaw and CircledLetter. Confidence intervals, significance tests, and repeated end-to-end searches are absent, although both the search agent and target LVLM may be stochastic. This makes the claimed exploration stability insufficiently supported.

The non-transferability conclusion is overstated by Table 4. The Gemini-discovered prompt improves all three models substantially, and the Claude-discovered prompt also improves all three over naive inference. The experiment demonstrates that the best prompt can be model-dependent and that one prompt can harm other models, but it does not establish that prompts are generally or rarely transferable. Moreover, this analysis covers only one synthetic task.

Reproducibility is incomplete. There is no algorithm pseudocode specifying tree traversal, visitation-count updates, duplicate-node handling, normalization of self-evaluation scores, tie-breaking, or final-prompt selection. The appendix's item labeled 'Implementation prompt' appears to be an idea-generation prompt and explicitly says another agent will update the code later; the actual code-generation/repair prompt is not supplied. API settings, sampling parameters, model version, exact evaluation prompts, and complete discovered programs are also missing.

The NUCT formulation is insufficiently justified. Its self-assessed gain and novelty scores come from an LLM but are not calibrated or independently validated, while the ablations jointly change substantial parts of the procedure. A direct standard-UCT ablation and separate tests of the gain, novelty, and saturation terms are needed to support the claimed selection contribution.

The efficiency analysis counts tokens but omits external-tool computation, API latency, image-model inference, and the execution of many development examples. Because SEVEX uses GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, and DepthAnything and incurs a large upfront search cost, token count alone does not establish overall computational or monetary efficiency.

Some benchmark improvements are modest, and SEVEX does not consistently win: it ties SketchPad on Depth and trails it on Visual Correspondence. The paper does not analyze whether task-specific gains arise from genuine improvements to LVLM perception, from external models effectively solving parts of the task, or from benchmark-specific heuristics.

The development sets contain only 30 examples, yet 50 adaptive iterations are conducted and the best strategy is selected. Although held-out test results mitigate direct overfitting, the paper lacks a principled model-selection protocol, validation curves, or sensitivity analysis for development-set size, search budget, and the four manually chosen hyperparameters.

Overall, this is a promising Algorithms/General contribution, but the limited baselines, one-backbone primary evaluation, incomplete reproducibility, and unsupported non-transferability claim leave the scientific case slightly below the acceptance threshold. These issues require broader controlled experiments rather than only editorial correction.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant problem: automatically discovering reusable, task-level visual prompts for LVLM perception failures, avoiding both manual prompt engineering and costly per-example program generation.

SEVEX has a coherent high-level design combining an abstract idea space, tree-based exploration, empirical evaluation, and semantic feedback. The discovered Jigsaw strategy—using depth-map discontinuities to evaluate candidate completions—is an interesting qualitative example of unconventional tool reuse.

The evaluation covers nine tasks from BlindTest and BLINK. On Gemini-2.5-Flash, SEVEX improves average test accuracy from 71.6% for naive inference and 64.6% for SketchPad to 78.9%, while reporting substantially lower inference cost than SketchPad. The paper also discloses development-set indices and several agent prompts.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the central algorithmic case is not adequately isolated. NUCT is compared only through broad removals such as “without tree structure”; there are no controlled comparisons against standard UCT, random or greedy search, novelty-only selection, or other agent/code-search methods under equal iteration and token budgets. Thus, the results do not establish that the proposed selection rule is responsible for the gains.

The main comparison is too narrow and potentially favorable to SEVEX. SketchPad and a custom SketchPad+APE variant are the only optimization baselines, despite substantial related work on automatic prompt optimization, evolutionary code search, and LLM tree-search agents. Moreover, task-level SEVEX consumes 50 labeled-development iterations before inference, whereas the naive and SketchPad results do not receive comparable task-level optimization; token accounting helps quantify this cost but does not substitute for stronger matched-budget baselines.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper does not clearly identify the models and decoding settings used for each Engineer and Analyst role, give the actual code-generation/implementation prompt, provide complete tool documentation or implementations, explain parsing and execution-error handling, or state whether code will be released. Appendix A even labels an apparent duplicate idea-generation prompt as the “Implementation prompt.” Key search details—including traversal, visitation-count updates, root scoring, normalization of self-evaluation scores, best-prompt selection, and tie handling—remain underspecified.

The empirical uncertainty is not characterized. Main test results appear to be single point estimates with no confidence intervals, repeated-search variance, or significance tests, despite stochastic model generation and repeated adaptive selection on only 30 development examples per task. The five-run ablation reports only mean curves without error bands and covers just two of nine tasks, so the broad claims of “significant” improvement and exploration stability are unsupported.

The claimed non-transferability conclusion is not justified by Table 4. It examines only one task, three models, and one discovered prompt per model. More importantly, the Gemini-derived prompt improves all three backbones substantially, and the Claude-derived prompt also improves both Gemini and Claude. These observations show model-dependent rankings, but they do not support the stronger claim that prompts are “rarely transferable.”

Several efficiency and method claims need tighter substantiation. Exploration cost is measured only in tokens even though object detection, segmentation, depth estimation, image processing, and repeated benchmark execution incur material compute and latency. The comparison does not report wall-clock time, API cost, external-model compute, failure rate, or the cost of five-run studies. Hyperparameters are presented without sensitivity analysis, and the search-budget choice is not justified.

The qualitative analysis is selective and provides no systematic taxonomy of discovered prompts, execution failures, or cases where optimization harms performance. SEVEX remains worse than naive inference on some task/model combinations, but these failures and the risks of development-set overfitting are not examined. Overall, the idea is promising, but missing controls, underspecified implementation, and overclaimed conclusions prevent a convincing ECCV-level case in the current form.

strengths: SEVEX addresses a relevant problem: automatically discovering reusable, task-level visual prompts, thereby amortizing exploration costs instead of generating tool-use code separately for every test sample.

The high-level idea space, novelty-guided tree search, and semantic backpropagation form a coherent framework. Separating conceptual strategies from low-level code is intuitive and potentially useful beyond the evaluated tasks.

The empirical gains are substantial: average accuracy increases from 71.6% for naive inference and 64.6% for SketchPad to 78.9%, while inference cost remains close to naive inference and far below per-sample SketchPad generation. The improvement is especially compelling on Line Intersections and Jigsaw.

The comparison with SketchPad+APE supports the value of optimizing visual transformations rather than only text prompts: SEVEX reports higher average test accuracy, much lower exploration cost, and a smaller development-to-test gap.

The qualitative results are informative and demonstrate nontrivial discoveries, particularly the use of depth-estimation discontinuities to evaluate Jigsaw completions. Prompts, development indices, tool interfaces, and several implementation details are included in the appendix.
The ablations averaged over five runs provide initial evidence that the abstract space, tree structure, and semantic feedback all contribute to exploration efficiency.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates and statistical tests despite repeatedly describing gains as significant. Most headline results appear to be single accuracy values from stochastic proprietary-model inference, and the manuscript does not report repeated test runs, confidence intervals, temperature, API snapshot, or test-set sample counts.

The central non-transferability claim is overstated by the presented evidence. Table 4 covers only one task and three prompts, while prompts 1 and 2 improve all three evaluated backbones substantially over their naive baselines. The table supports model-dependent rankings, but not the stronger assertion that prompts are rarely transferable.

Baselines for the proposed search algorithm are too limited. SketchPad+APE optimizes a text prompt and is not a direct alternative for structured visual-prompt search. Comparisons against random search, greedy or beam search, standard MCTS/UCT, or a matched-budget LLM optimizer are needed to isolate the benefit of NUCT and semantic backpropagation.

The component ablation is restricted to two of nine tasks and reports only development-set curves. It provides no uncertainty bands, final test performance, sensitivity to the four search hyperparameters, or separate analysis of the self-evaluated gain and novelty scores.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The paper supplies meta-prompts and development indices but not full discovered programs, exact model/tool versions and configurations, decoding settings, complete selection protocol, or executable code. It is also unclear how the five exploration runs relate to the prompts and test scores in the main tables.

Some claims conflate improving intrinsic LVLM perception with delegating perception to external pretrained models such as GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, and DepthAnything. A breakdown by tool category, including a no-external-model setting, would clarify whether SEVEX repairs the target model's visual reasoning or mainly discovers effective task pipelines.

The cost analysis counts tokens but omits external-model computation, image-processing runtime, API pricing, and the cost of failed executions. Consequently, the claimed overall cost advantage is only partially established.

Assessed as Algorithms/General because no contribution type is declared. The paper is practically promising and supports a borderline acceptance, but stronger controlled search baselines and more rigorous, reproducible evaluation are needed for a clearly convincing algorithmic contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: automatically discovering reusable, task-specific visual interventions for LVLM perception failures, avoiding both manual prompt engineering and per-example program generation.

SEVEX is a coherent framework combining an abstract idea space, novelty-guided tree search, executable visual prompts, and sample-level semantic feedback. The separation of high-level ideas from code is intuitive and potentially useful.

The reported gains are substantial: average accuracy rises from 71.6% for naive inference and 64.6% for SketchPad to 78.9%, while inference token cost remains close to naive inference. Improvements are demonstrated on nine tasks spanning BlindTest and BLINK.

The evaluation includes useful breadth and analysis: additional GPT-4o and Claude backbones, component ablations averaged over five runs, a restricted-toolbox experiment, development-split sensitivity, qualitative prompts, and prompt-transfer experiments.

Some discovered solutions are genuinely interesting, such as using depth-estimation discontinuities to solve Jigsaw. The restricted-toolbox results also provide evidence that improvements do not arise solely from access to powerful external vision models.
The manuscript is generally well organized, clearly motivated, and visually communicates the search procedure and discovered strategies.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that standard, the principal empirical comparison does not isolate the proposed search algorithm: SketchPad is a per-sample tool-use method, while SketchPad+APE optimizes text around SketchPad. There is no equal-budget comparison against random or best-of-N search, iterative LLM refinement, evolutionary search, standard UCT/MCTS, or another program/prompt-search agent. Thus the results convincingly support task-wise optimization, but less conclusively support SEVEX's specific search design.

The core algorithm is underspecified. It is unclear whether selection traverses the tree recursively or scores all nodes globally, how visits are updated when an already executed node is selected, and precisely how selection leads to expansion. Equation 2 is undefined when a parent has no executed children unless an unstated smoothing or initialization rule is used. These omissions impede both technical assessment and reproduction.

Ablations of the abstract space, tree search, and semantic backpropagation cover only two of nine tasks. The variants are not defined precisely, and exact numerical results are provided only as plots. This limited evidence is insufficient to establish that each component is broadly necessary, especially given the stochastic agentic pipeline.

Most headline results appear to come from a single discovery run. Statistical uncertainty is absent for the main test results, and development-split sensitivity is examined only for CircledLetter. With just 30 development examples and repeated adaptive evaluation over 50 iterations, overfitting and run-to-run selection variance remain important concerns for the other tasks.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper does not provide the full discovered programs and text prompts, complete tool implementations/configurations, decoding parameters, precise proprietary model versions, or sufficient execution details. The qualitative code is explicitly simplified, so the reported system cannot be reconstructed from the manuscript.

The efficiency comparison measures only LVLM tokens and does not account for external-model computation, latency, or monetary cost from GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, and DepthAnything. Exploration also costs roughly 3,442 naive inferences, limiting applicability to high-volume, stationary tasks; this constraint deserves more prominent treatment.

The claimed non-transferability is overstated. Table 4 actually shows that prompts found for other models can substantially improve some backbones—for example, the Gemini prompt raises GPT-4o from 8.2% to 59.1%, exceeding GPT-4o's own discovered prompt at 57.1%. The evidence more directly supports model-dependent ranking than a general lack of transferability.

The experimental scope is restricted to nine benchmark tasks with fixed query formats and tools. There is no evaluation under distribution shift, on broader real-world perception tasks, or when task labels and failure modes are less cleanly specified, leaving the generality of task-wise visual-prompt discovery uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: automatically discovering reusable, task-level visual interventions for LVLM perception failures, avoiding expensive per-example program generation.

Searching over high-level ideas, translating them into executable visual prompts, and feeding sample-level experimental diagnoses back into the search is an intuitive and potentially useful framework.

The reported held-out results are substantial: SEVEX improves average accuracy from 71.6% to 78.9% on the nine primary tasks while using far fewer inference tokens than SketchPad. Full discovery on GPT-4o and Claude also provides useful evidence beyond the primary Gemini backbone.

The restricted-toolbox experiment is informative: basic image and drawing operations retain the BlindTest gains, suggesting that improvements are not solely inherited from powerful pretrained vision tools. The appendix also supplies the agent prompts and exact development indices.
weaknesses: I assess this undeclared contribution as Algorithms/General. The most important algorithmic claims are not adequately isolated. Comparisons are limited to naive inference, SketchPad, and text-prompt APE; there is no controlled random search, best-of-N, greedy search, standard UCT/MCTS, or flat semantic-search baseline operating with the same idea generator, toolbox, development budget, and feedback. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that NUCT—or even the proposed tree search—is responsible for the main gains rather than repeated LLM sampling and development-set selection.

The central non-transferability conclusion is contradicted by Table 4. The Gemini-discovered prompt improves all three models substantially, including GPT-4o from 8.2% to 59.1%, and the Claude-discovered prompt also improves all three. Moreover, the Gemini prompt slightly outperforms the GPT-specific prompt on GPT-4o (59.1% versus 57.1%). The results support variation in which prompt is optimal, but not the repeated claim that prompts are 'rarely transferable' or that every model requires independent discovery.

The ablation evidence is too narrow for a nine-task paper. Search-component ablations are shown only for Jigsaw and CircledLetter, only as development-accuracy curves, without endpoint tables, test accuracy, variance bands, or statistical comparisons. Thus the contribution of the abstract space, semantic backpropagation, and tree search to held-out performance remains uncertain.

The evaluation repeatedly selects among 50 trials using only 30 development examples, making adaptive overfitting a serious concern. Split sensitivity is examined only for CircledLetter. Primary test results lack repeated-discovery variance, confidence intervals, significance tests, and per-task test-set sizes, despite claims of significant improvement and exploration stability.

The method is insufficiently specified for reproduction. It does not clearly define tree traversal and visitation updates, root handling, zero-count cases in Eq. 2, duplicate-node handling, normalization/rescaling of self-evaluation scores, representative-image selection, answer parsing, execution-error handling, or final-prompt selection. The actual discovered task prompts and executable implementations are also not provided in full.

The efficiency analysis counts tokens but omits wall-clock time, monetary cost, external-model computation, and hardware. SEVEX still requires roughly 3,442 naive inferences of upfront exploration per task, so its practical advantage depends on a large deployment volume. Comparing token counts alone is especially incomplete when some prompts invoke GroundingDINO, SemanticSAM, or DepthAnything.

Originality is moderate rather than compelling: the framework largely combines familiar LLM-agent prompt optimization, tree search/UCB-style selection, self-evaluation, and verbal feedback, then applies them to programmatic visual prompting. Given the missing controlled search baselines and limited ablations, the manuscript does not yet demonstrate that its specific algorithmic design constitutes a sufficiently validated ECCV contribution.

strengths: Treating the submission as Algorithms/General, it addresses a timely and practically important problem: automating task- and model-specific visual-prompt discovery instead of relying on manual trial-and-error or costly per-sample tool generation.

SEVEX is a coherent framework: it separates high-level ideas from code, uses novelty-guided tree search, and propagates sample-level semantic feedback. This combination is intuitive and yields interesting strategies, including the unconventional use of depth estimation for Jigsaw.

The main empirical gains are compelling. Across nine BlindTest/BLINK tasks with Gemini-2.5-flash, SEVEX improves average accuracy from 71.6% for naive inference and 64.6% for SketchPad to 78.9%, while using far fewer inference tokens than SketchPad.

The evaluation includes useful breadth beyond the headline comparison: full discovery on GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.0, component ablations, a restricted-toolbox study, qualitative search trees, development-split sensitivity, and token-cost accounting.

Reproducibility is helped by reporting the development indices, tool inventory, hyperparameters, and detailed agent prompts in the appendix.
